qs.q: A pathologist distinguishes a simple lymphangioma from a capillary hemangioma in a head and neck lesion. Which specific feature confirms the lymphatic origin?
o: Rapid growth following minor trauma with ulceration
Presence of intravascular thrombosis with dystrophic calcification
Expression of lymphatic endothelial markers such as VEGFR-3 or LYVE-1
Large, dilated vascular channels separated by connective tissue stroma
qs.e: Lymphangiomas are distinguished from hemangiomas by the presence of lymphatic endothelial markers like VEGFR-3 and LYVE-1. Thrombosis with calcification is characteristic of cavernous hemangiomas.

qs.q: Cavernous hemangiomas are distinguished from capillary hemangiomas by which of the following features?
o: They are exclusively found in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
They are more infiltrative, do not spontaneously regress, and often show intravascular thrombosis
They are composed of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma
They are the most common type of hemangioma in infancy
qs.e: Cavernous hemangiomas are infiltrative, do not regress, and often have thrombosis/calcification. Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type and consist of thin-walled capillaries.
